title: Risk Management, Quality, and Safety Systems

concepts.title: Spend your worry where it multiplies
concepts.mechanism: A risk register full of entries is useless if every entry gets the same attention — you have finite mitigation budget and finite hours, and they should go where probability and impact multiply into the biggest number, not where the loudest person is worried. A hurricane threatening an open excavation is both likely (it's hurricane season) and severe (flooded, collapsed works) — that gets real mitigation money. A minor nuisance complaint that's unlikely and low-impact does not deserve the same register entry's worth of attention, even though both 'feel like risks.'
concepts.mechanismPro: Score every register entry as probability × impact, with a named owner, a mitigation action, and a date; re-score on a fixed cadence — the register is a prioritization tool, not a worry journal, and its value is in what it tells you NOT to spend time on.
concepts.hook: A doctor doesn't treat a paper cut and a heart attack with the same urgency just because both are 'injuries.' Triage means sending your attention where probability and severity multiply highest.

applied.prompt: Your risk register has 40 entries. You have limited time this week. How do you decide what to work on?

options.label: Rank all 40 by probability × impact and work the top of that list first
options.outcome: Right. This is exactly what the matrix is for — it turns 40 undifferentiated worries into a prioritized, defensible work order.

options.label: Work whichever risks were raised most recently or most loudly
options.outcome: This spends real mitigation time on recency and volume instead of actual exposure — often the opposite of where the register says the danger is.

options.label: Give each of the 40 entries equal attention this week
options.outcome: Spreading finite attention evenly across risks with wildly different exposure means the highest-probability, highest-impact items get the same thin slice as a near-zero one.

applied.debrief: This is the same 'spend where it counts' discipline as M09's tiered contingency — both refuse to treat all risk lines the same, because blending them hides exactly the ones that deserve real money and attention.

summary: Three systems that run continuously under everything else: a live risk register (probability × impact, owner, mitigation, date), a quality system enforced at hold points and verified by independent testing, and a safety program whose record flows directly into your insurance costs and regulator standing. Plus the honest answer to 'what do I directly manage': fewer things, better systems.

sections.heading: The risk register method
sections.body: Identify → score (probability × impact, 1–5 scales) → assign an OWNER → mitigation with a DATE → track, reviewed monthly. The project's pre-loaded top risks: (1) hurricane strike during construction; (2) EIA/CEC delay pushing the marine window a full year — the critical path's critical path; (3) rock/karst quantity variance; (4) the island's labor supply ceiling; (5) long-lead procurement; (6) sales absorption below pro forma — phase gates must let you throttle starts without stranding infrastructure; (7) downdrift erosion / neighbor litigation on the groins; (8) WSC/BPL capacity timing; (9) fuel/marina environmental incident; (10) KEY-PERSON DEPENDENCY — you. Document systems so the project survives your absence.

sections.heading: The quality system
sections.body: Quality is DEFINED in documents (specs + approved submittals + shop drawings), ENFORCED at hold points (no pour without your rep's sign-off at footing rebar, ring beam, suspended slab, roof strapping; no cover-up of MEP without rough sign-off), VERIFIED by independent testing (concrete cylinders, density, asphalt cores, weld/bolt inspection on marine structures — the lab contracts to the OWNER), and MEASURED: first-pass inspection rate per sub is your quality KPI, published to the subs. Marine QC additions: bathymetric surveys to verify dredge depths (you pay per cy — the survey is how you avoid paying for water), stone gradation certs on armor, bulkhead alignment tolerances.

sections.heading: Safety, and what it buys
sections.body: The Health and Safety at Work Act is the floor; your program sits above it: site induction for every worker, fall protection on all condo frame work, excavation/edge protection at the canals — open water + heavy equipment + rock edges is the site's likeliest fatality mechanism, so canal-edge protocols get treated as seriously as anything on the project — marine ops plan (vessel traffic, diver operations during dredging), the hurricane action plan rehearsed before June 1 every year, and incident investigation with root cause. Your safety record flows directly into insurance premiums and your standing with regulators.

quiz.teach: A risk register entry isn't complete with just a description and a score.
quiz.prompt: What turns a risk register from a worry list into a management tool?

choices.text: Every risk gets an OWNER and a mitigation with a DATE, reviewed monthly — unowned risks with undated mitigations are just documented anxiety
choices.why: Correct. Probability × impact prioritizes; owner + date makes something happen. The monthly review is where 'mitigation planned' either became 'mitigation done' or gets escalated.

choices.text: Scoring precision — using 1–10 scales instead of 1–5
choices.why: Finer scales add false precision to estimates that are judgment calls anyway. The action fields (owner, date) are what move risk.

choices.text: Longer lists — capturing every conceivable risk
choices.why: A 300-line register nobody reads manages nothing. Ten owned, dated, tracked risks beat a hundred documented ones.

choices.text: Quantifying every risk in dollars
choices.why: Dollar estimates help on the big ones, but plenty of real risks (regulator standing, key-person) resist honest quantification — and still need owners and dates.

quiz.explanation: The register's pre-loaded top ten for this project ranges from hurricanes to your own irreplaceability. Note risk #2 — EIA/CEC delay — is called 'the critical path's critical path': it's why the environmental workstream starts before everything else.

quiz.teach: A hold point is a stage where work legally may not proceed without a designated sign-off.
quiz.prompt: Which stages are EVERY-house hold points on this project?

choices.text: Footing rebar, ring beam, roof strapping, and MEP rough before cover-up
choices.why: Correct — the structural and concealed stages where an error becomes invisible and permanent. Finish tolerances, by contrast, get QC by sampling.

choices.text: Every stage of every house
choices.why: Inspecting everything everywhere is a staffing fantasy that collapses into inspecting nothing well. Hold points concentrate scrutiny where errors hide.

choices.text: Only the stages MOW inspects
choices.why: MOW's inspections are the code minimum. Your hold points overlap but serve YOU — they exist so your money never covers up an unverified stage.

choices.text: Paint, trim, and final finishes
choices.why: Finish defects are visible and fixable — sampling handles them. Hold points guard what disappears: rebar under concrete, strapping under roofing, pipe behind drywall.

quiz.explanation: The logic: hold points for what gets CONCEALED (structure, MEP rough), sampling for what stays visible (finishes). No pour, no cover-up, without sign-off — and the first-pass rate per sub, published as a league table, is your quality KPI.

quiz.teach: Dredging is paid per cubic yard removed — measured somehow.
quiz.prompt: Why does the owner commission independent bathymetric surveys during dredging?

choices.text: Because you pay per cy — pre- and post-dredge surveys of the actual bottom are how you avoid paying for water
choices.why: Correct. Without independent surveys, the payable quantity is whatever the contractor's records say it is. The survey is the marine QA lab.

choices.text: DEPP requires them for the EMP
choices.why: The EMP has its own monitoring, but the survey's commercial role — verifying payable quantities — is why the OWNER commissions it.

choices.text: For navigation chart updates
choices.why: Charts eventually update, but that's a Port Department byproduct, not why your QS wants the data monthly.

choices.text: To find archaeology before it stops the dredge
choices.why: Archaeological screening happens in the EIA phase. The recurring surveys are about cubic yards and dollars.

quiz.explanation: Same principle as the land-side testing lab, wetter: independent measurement, contracted to the owner, of every quantity you pay against. Marine QC also adds stone gradation certificates on armor and alignment tolerances on bulkheads.

quiz.teach: Every site has a 'likeliest fatality mechanism' — the hazard geometry most likely to kill someone. Naming it focuses the program.
quiz.prompt: What is this site's likeliest fatality mechanism?

choices.text: The canal edges — open water + heavy equipment + rock edges, for years of construction
choices.why: Correct. An excavator working a rock edge over deep water, daily, across miles of canal, for years — canal-edge protocols get treated as seriously as anything on the project.

choices.text: Falls from the condo frames
choices.why: The classic construction killer, and fall protection on frame work is mandatory — but the condos are 3–4 storeys with standard controls. The canals are an unusual, persistent, site-wide hazard.

choices.text: Blasting operations
choices.why: Dramatic but tightly proceduralized and episodic — licensed blaster, exclusion zones, scheduled shots. The canal edge is there every unremarkable day.

choices.text: Hurricane events
choices.why: Storms threaten property at scale, but the preparedness plan evacuates people. The daily drowning-and-crushing geometry of the canal edges is the persistent human risk.

quiz.explanation: Risk thinking 101: frequency × exposure × severity. The canal edges score high on all three for years, which is why edge protection, equipment setback rules, and water-rescue provisions belong in every relevant sub's contract, not just the safety manual.

quiz.teach: Risk #10 on the project register is you.
quiz.prompt: What is the mitigation for key-person dependency on the owner-developer?

choices.text: Document the systems — registers, logs, pipelines, procedures — so the project survives your absence; and direct-manage fewer things with better systems
choices.why: Correct, and it's the same answer as 'what do I directly manage': the value isn't your daily presence in every decision, it's the machine you build that makes decisions repeatable.

choices.text: Key-person life insurance
choices.why: Insurance pays money; it doesn't run the permit pipeline. Financial mitigation without operational mitigation leaves the project rich and rudderless.

choices.text: Hire a deputy who shadows everything
choices.why: A shadow of undocumented judgment inherits the same fragility. The deputy plus documented systems works; the deputy instead of them doesn't.

choices.text: Avoid vacations during construction
choices.why: That's not mitigation, that's maximizing exposure to the risk — a burned-out key person is the failure mode arriving early.

quiz.explanation: This is the register's most personal entry and its most honest: a project that only works when you're in the room is a fragile project. Every system this app teaches — committed-cost reports, hold points, logs, pipelines — is also the succession plan.

mathProblems.title: Scoring a risk
mathProblems.context: Risk score = probability × impact on 1–5 scales. A 4×4 risk (16+) demands an owner and a mitigation date this week; a 2×2 gets watched monthly.

decisionPoints.title: The Friday pour
decisionPoints.scenario: Friday, 3 PM. The concrete sub has a pump, a crew, and eight ring beams formed and ready on Phase 2's first street. Your inspector — the hold-point sign-off for ring beam rebar — went home sick at noon and can't be reached. The sub's foreman says his own guys checked the steel and it's fine: 'We pour now or you pay for a Saturday crew and a pump remob. Your call.'

options.label: No sign-off, no pour. Pay the Saturday premium and get the inspector (or a qualified substitute) there in the morning
options.outcome: The Saturday costs real money and buys something priceless: the hold-point system stays real. Saturday's inspection finds two beams with missing corner bars at column intersections — the exact hurricane-critical detail the hold point exists for. Every sub on site hears both halves of this story.

options.label: Pour on the foreman's word — he's experienced and the steel is probably fine
options.outcome: Probably. And the hold-point system just became advisory: every future Friday afternoon now has this precedent, the sub's crews learn your sign-offs bend under schedule pressure, and if any of those eight beams is wrong, it's wrong inside concrete, in the wind structure, on all eight houses.

options.label: Have the foreman photo-document every beam against the drawings, review remotely, then pour
options.outcome: Better than nothing, worse than eyes: photos miss what inspections catch (bar laps, chair heights, ties at intersections — the three-dimensional stuff). As a one-off documented exception with your explicit remote review, defensible; as a habit, it's the slow death of the hold point.

decisionPoints.debrief: Hold points only work if they hold under pressure — and the pressure always arrives at 3 PM Friday with a pump on the clock. The cost of enforcing the system is always visible and always small; the cost of the exception is invisible until it's structural. Pay the Saturday.

decisionPoints.title: The near-miss at the canal edge
decisionPoints.scenario: An excavator working the canal cut slides half a track over the rock edge — operator unhurt, machine recovered, nobody outside the earthworks crew saw it. The sub's superintendent calls it 'a non-event, ground just spalled a little' and doesn't want it written up: 'incident reports raise everyone's premiums for nothing.'

options.label: Treat it as the free lesson it is: formal near-miss report, root-cause investigation (why was the machine that close? was the edge setback rule followed? was the rock undercut?), findings to every crew on the water
options.outcome: The investigation finds the edge setback rule existed but was never marked physically — paint and barriers go up the same week, canal-wide. The near-miss that cost nothing just rewrote the protocol that prevents the fatality version. This is what 'incident investigation with root cause' means when it matters.

options.label: Skip the paperwork; have a quiet word with the operator about staying back from the edge
options.outcome: The systemic cause — unmarked setbacks on undercut rock — stays in place for every other operator on eight miles of canal. Near-misses are the cheapest safety data that exists; unrecorded, this one is just a story that predicts a funeral.

options.label: Log it minimally to keep the record technically complete, no investigation
options.outcome: The log entry satisfies the file and teaches nothing. When the serious version happens later, the minimal entry becomes evidence you knew about edge instability and investigated nothing — worse for the premiums, and the regulator, than the honest version would ever have been.

decisionPoints.debrief: The canal edge is this site's likeliest fatality mechanism, and near-misses are its early-warning system. A safety culture is measured by what it does with events that cost nothing — and your incident record flows into insurance pricing and regulator standing either way, so let it flow as evidence of a system that learns.
